CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER

Random variables

A spinner at the school fair, a dice game at the funfair, insurance for your bike: behind every random experiment there are numbers, wins, losses, counts. Here you learn to calculate with these numbers. The expected value tells you what comes out in the long run, the standard deviation how much it varies.

12 LESSONS3 UNITSRATING GAMES OF CHANCE
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • define a random variable and give its probability distribution as a table and a bar chart
  • translate “exactly”, “at most” and “at least” into probabilities
  • calculate and interpret the expected value, the variance and the standard deviation
  • decide whether a game is fair

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Random variable and probability distribution

Three coins are tossed. There are 8 equally likely outcomes, from HHH to TTT. We are only interested in: how many heads?

The number $X$ = “number of heads” depends on chance and can take the values 0, 1, 2, 3. Counting the outcomes gives:

$x_i$0123
$P(X = x_i)$$\tfrac18$$\tfrac38$$\tfrac38$$\tfrac18$
KEY POINT · RANDOM VARIABLE

A random variable $X$ assigns a real number to every outcome of a random experiment.

The probability distribution of $X$ gives the probability $P(X = x_i)$ for every value $x_i$. All of them together add up to 1. It is shown as a table, a bar chart or a histogram.

“exactly $k$”: $P(X = k)$ · “at most $k$”: $P(X \le k)$ · “at least $k$”: $P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k - 1)$

A random variable is called discrete if it only takes single, countable values, for example counts or amounts of money.

Complementary event: “at least one” is almost always calculated via $1 - P(\text{none})$.

FIGURE · TOTAL SCORE OF TWO DICE

The height of the bars is $P(X = k)$, from $\tfrac{1}{36}$ at 2 and 12 up to $\tfrac{6}{36}$ at 7.

EXAMPLE 1 · TOTAL SCORE

$X$ is the total score of two dice. Calculate $P(X = 7)$, $P(X \le 4)$ and $P(X \ge 10)$.

$P(X = 7) = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$ · $P(X \le 4) = \tfrac{1 + 2 + 3}{36} = \tfrac16$ · $P(X \ge 10) = \tfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{36} = \tfrac16$

EXAMPLE 2 · DRAWING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

Two balls are drawn without replacement from an urn with 3 red and 2 blue balls. $X$ = number of red ones. Give the distribution.

$P(X = 0) = \tfrac25 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{10}$, $P(X = 2) = \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac{3}{10}$, $P(X = 1) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{10} - \tfrac{3}{10} = \tfrac{6}{10}$

EXERCISES

Four coins are tossed, $X$ = number of heads. Give the probability distribution.

There are 16 outcomes. How many of them have exactly two heads?

$P(X = 0) = \tfrac{1}{16}$, $P(X = 1) = \tfrac{4}{16}$, $P(X = 2) = \tfrac{6}{16}$, $P(X = 3) = \tfrac{4}{16}$, $P(X = 4) = \tfrac{1}{16}$

Fill in the missing probability and calculate $P(X \ge 2)$.

$x_i$0123
$P(X = x_i)$0.10.3?0.2

$1 - 0.1 - 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.4$, $P(X \ge 2) = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6$

A dice is rolled twice, $X$ is the larger of the two scores. Find the distribution of $X$.

$P(X = k) = \tfrac{2k - 1}{36}$: $\tfrac{1}{36}, \tfrac{3}{36}, \tfrac{5}{36}, \tfrac{7}{36}, \tfrac{9}{36}, \tfrac{11}{36}$ for $k = 1, \ldots, 6$. Reason: both dice at most $k$ in $k^2$ cases, at most $k - 1$ in $(k - 1)^2$ cases, the difference is $2k - 1$.

A spinner has three sectors with the angles at the centre 180°, 120° and 60°. They pay out €0, €2 and €5. Give the distribution of the payout and draw a bar chart.

$P(0) = \tfrac{180}{360} = \tfrac12$, $P(2) = \tfrac{120}{360} = \tfrac13$, $P(5) = \tfrac{60}{360} = \tfrac16$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2The expected value

800 people play the spinner at the school fair. About 400 get nothing, 200 get €1 each, 100 get €2 each and 100 get €10 each. That is €$200 + 200 + 1000 = 1400$, so on average $\tfrac{1400}{800} = 1.75$ euros per game.

You get the same without the 800 people, straight from the distribution: $0 \cdot \tfrac12 + 1 \cdot \tfrac14 + 2 \cdot \tfrac18 + 10 \cdot \tfrac18 = 1.75$. With a stake of €2 you lose 25 cents per game on average, the class fund makes money.

KEY POINT · EXPECTED VALUE

If $X$ takes the values $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, the expected value is $$E(X) = \mu = x_1 \cdot P(X = x_1) + x_2 \cdot P(X = x_2) + \ldots + x_n \cdot P(X = x_n).$$

It is the mean in the long run: after very many repetitions the mean of the results is close to $E(X)$.

If $X$ is the gain (payout minus stake), a game is called fair if $E(X) = 0$.

Not a possible value: the expected value when rolling a dice is 3.5. This score never comes up, it is a mean.

Centre of mass: if you imagine the bars of the bar chart as weights on a seesaw, the pivot is at $\mu$.

INTERACTIVE · RANDOM VARIABLES AND THEIR KEY FIGURES

Choose an example. Then play 10, 100 or 1,000 times and compare the mean of your games with the expected value.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE DICE

Calculate the expected value of the score of a dice.

$E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) \cdot \tfrac16 = \tfrac{21}{6} = 3.5$

EXAMPLE 4 · CHUCK-A-LUCK

You bet €1 on a number, then three dice are rolled. For every dice showing your number you win €1, if none shows it, your stake is lost. Is the game fair?

No match: $\left(\tfrac56\right)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$, one: $3 \cdot \tfrac16 \cdot \left(\tfrac56\right)^2 = \tfrac{75}{216}$, two: $\tfrac{15}{216}$, three: $\tfrac{1}{216}$.

$E(X) = \dfrac{-125 + 75 + 2 \cdot 15 + 3 \cdot 1}{216} = -\dfrac{17}{216} \approx -0.079$. Unfair: a loss of almost 8 cents per game.

EXERCISES

Calculate $E(X)$ for the distribution $x_i$: 0, 1, 2, 3 with $P(X = x_i)$: 0.1; 0.3; 0.4; 0.2.

$0 + 0.3 + 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.7$

Calculate the expected value of the number of heads with three coins. Interpret the result.

$0 \cdot \tfrac18 + 1 \cdot \tfrac38 + 2 \cdot \tfrac38 + 3 \cdot \tfrac18 = \tfrac{12}{8} = 1.5$. On average, three tosses give heads 1.5 times.

The spinner at the school fair is to become fair. a) How high would the stake have to be? b) The stake stays at €2. What amount must the €10 sector pay out then?

a) €1.75   b) $0.25 + 0.25 + \tfrac{a}{8} = 2 \Rightarrow a = 12$ euros

A raffle sells 1,000 tickets at €2 each. There is one prize of €500, 10 prizes of €50 and 100 prizes of €5. Calculate the expected value of the gain for one ticket.

Payout on average $\tfrac{500 + 500 + 500}{1000} = 1.5$ euros. Gain $1.5 - 2 = -0.5$ euros. The raffle takes in €500.

A bike worth €800 is stolen with a probability of 3% per year. What annual premium would be fair? An insurance company charges €39. Why do many people take out insurance all the same?

Fair premium $800 \cdot 0.03 = 24$ euros. The €15 difference covers the costs and the profit of the insurance company. You pay a small, certain amount to protect yourself against a large, unlikely loss.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Variance and standard deviation

In game A you win or lose €1 with equal probability. In game B you win €99 with a probability of 1%, otherwise you lose €1. Both have the expected value 0. All the same, game B feels completely different.

The difference lies in the spread: in game A every result is €1 away from the expected value, in game B it is mostly €1, but rarely €99. The spread is measured with the mean of the squared deviations from the expected value.

KEY POINT · VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION

Variance: $V(X) = (x_1 - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_1) + \ldots + (x_n - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_n)$

Standard deviation: $\sigma = \sqrt{V(X)}$. It has the same unit as $X$ and tells you how far the values typically deviate from the expected value.

Game A: $V = 1$, $\sigma = 1$ · Game B: $V = 99^2 \cdot 0.01 + (-1)^2 \cdot 0.99 = 99$, $\sigma \approx 9.95$

Shortcut: often quicker is $V(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2$, that is “mean of the squares minus square of the mean”.

Risk: in finance, the standard deviation is used as a measure of the risk of an investment.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE DICE

Calculate the variance and the standard deviation of the score of a dice.

With $\mu = 3.5$: $V(X) = \tfrac16 \left(2.5^2 + 1.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 1.5^2 + 2.5^2\right) = \tfrac{17.5}{6} \approx 2.917$, $\sigma \approx 1.708$

EXAMPLE 6 · TWO FILLING MACHINES

Machine 1 fills 498 g, 500 g, 502 g with 0.1; 0.8; 0.1. Machine 2 fills 495 g, 500 g, 505 g with 0.2; 0.6; 0.2. Which one works more precisely?

Both: $\mu = 500$ g. $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{4 \cdot 0.1 + 4 \cdot 0.1} = \sqrt{0.8} \approx 0.89$ g, $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{25 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 2} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$ g. Machine 1 has less spread.

EXERCISES

Calculate $V(X)$ and $\sigma$ for the number of heads with three coins ($\mu = 1.5$).

$V = 2.25 \cdot \tfrac18 + 0.25 \cdot \tfrac38 + 0.25 \cdot \tfrac38 + 2.25 \cdot \tfrac18 = \tfrac68 = 0.75$, $\sigma \approx 0.866$

$X$ takes 0, 2 and 4 with 0.25; 0.5; 0.25. Calculate $\mu$, $V(X)$ and $\sigma$.

$\mu = 2$, $V = 4 \cdot 0.25 + 0 + 4 \cdot 0.25 = 2$, $\sigma = \sqrt2 \approx 1.414$

Compare chuck-a-luck (example 4) with game A from the introduction: calculate the standard deviation of the gain in chuck-a-luck. Use the widget to check.

$E(X^2) = \tfrac{125 + 75 + 4 \cdot 15 + 9}{216} = \tfrac{269}{216} \approx 1.2454$, $V = 1.2454 - 0.0787^2 \approx 1.239$, $\sigma \approx 1.113$ euros

Show with the example of the dice that $V(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2$ gives the same as the definition.

$E(X^2) = \tfrac{1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36}{6} = \tfrac{91}{6} \approx 15.167$, minus $3.5^2 = 12.25$ gives $\tfrac{35}{12} \approx 2.917$. As in example 5.

TEST YOURSELF!

$X$ takes 0 and 10 with 0.5 each. What is $\sigma$?

$\mu = 5$, $V = 25$, $\sigma = 5$

$V(X) = 2.25$. What is the standard deviation?

$\sqrt{2.25} = 1.5$

Two games have the same expected value, game A has $\sigma = €2$, game B has $\sigma = €8$. Which one is riskier?

In game B the results typically deviate much more from the expected value.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Explain without a long calculation why the total score of two dice has the expected value 7.

The distribution is symmetric about 7. Or: each dice has the expected value 3.5, and expected values add up.

How many euros do you lose in the long run in 216 games of chuck-a-luck? How many in 1,000?

216 games: about €17. 1,000 games: $1000 \cdot \tfrac{17}{216} \approx 78.70$ euros.

Connecting with chapter 1.1: from an urn with 3 red and 2 blue balls you draw two without replacement. For every red one you get €1. The stake is €1. Is the game fair?

With example 2: $E(\text{payout}) = 0 \cdot 0.1 + 1 \cdot 0.6 + 2 \cdot 0.3 = 1.2$ euros. Average gain $+0.20$ euros: favourable for the player. A stake of €1.20 would be fair.

Dice game: with a six you win $a$ euros, otherwise you lose €1. For which $a$ is the game fair? What is $\sigma$ then?

$\tfrac{a}{6} - \tfrac56 = 0 \Rightarrow a = 5$. $V = 25 \cdot \tfrac16 + 1 \cdot \tfrac56 = 5$, $\sigma = \sqrt5 \approx 2.24$ euros.

EXCURSIONA GAME WITH AN INFINITE EXPECTED VALUE

The St Petersburg game

A coin is tossed until tails comes up for the first time. If that happens on the $k$-th toss, you get $2^k$ euros. With probability $\tfrac12$ you get €2, with $\tfrac14$ you get €4, with $\tfrac18$ you get €8, and so on.

The expected value is $2 \cdot \tfrac12 + 4 \cdot \tfrac14 + 8 \cdot \tfrac18 + \ldots = 1 + 1 + 1 + \ldots$, that is infinite. All the same, hardly anyone would pay a stake of more than €20. Why?

Nicolaus I Bernoulli asked the question in 1713 in a letter to Pierre Rémond de Montmort. His cousin Daniel Bernoulli answered in 1738: people do not value money by its amount but by its utility, and that grows more slowly than the amount. On top of that, no bank in the world could pay out the huge prizes of the rare long runs.

Source: Daniel Bernoulli: Specimen theoriae novae de mensura sortis. Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae 5 (1738).

RANDOM VARIABLE

Assigns a number to every outcome. Distribution: all $P(X = x_i)$, total 1.

EXPECTED VALUE

$E(X) = \mu = \sum x_i \cdot P(X = x_i)$, the mean in the long run.

Dice: 3.5 · Spinner: €1.75

FAIR GAME

Expected value of the gain equal to 0.

Chuck-a-luck: $-\tfrac{17}{216}$ euros, unfair

VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION

$V(X) = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(X = x_i)$, $\sigma = \sqrt{V(X)}$

Dice: $V \approx 2.917$, $\sigma \approx 1.708$
